cards.title: Octet rule check: spot the electron-deficient centre

walkthrough.question:
Three molecules are listed. Decide which ones have every atom ending up with a full octet of valence electrons.
I. NF3
II. BF3
III. PCl3
A. I and II only
B. I and III only
C. II and III only
D. I, II and III
walkthrough.key_idea: Boron has only three valence electrons: BF3 leaves B with six.
walkthrough.careful: Count electrons around the central atom, not bonds.
procedure: Count valence electrons for the whole molecule.
Join terminal atoms to the central atom with single bonds.
Complete each terminal atom's octet with lone pairs.
Put leftover electrons on the central atom as lone pairs.
Count electrons around each atom: eight means octet obeyed.
tricks: Group 13 centre (B, Al) with three bonds has only six electrons.
Group 15 centre with three single bonds keeps a lone pair: octet. Fails for PCl5.
if_lost: How many valence electrons does each central atom bring?
After three single bonds, how many electrons surround N, B and P?
Which central atoms still have a lone pair left over?

1_context.short: Octet check: SL Lewis formulas, including electron-deficient atoms.
1_context.why: The guide says molecules with fewer than an octet must be covered, so a BF3-type molecule is fair game next to normal ones.
1_context.avoid: Assuming every stable molecule obeys the octet rule; many candidates did (25M.1A.SL.TZ1.9).
1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.2.1: Lewis formulas for up to four electron pairs; octet rule; species with fewer than an octet included.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books drill octet-obeying examples; exams hide one exception among formulas that look alike.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Only B falls short of eight, so the answer excludes II.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Boron uses its three electrons in three bonds and has no lone pair, so its valence shell holds six electrons.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Picking D because all three look like simple AX3 molecules (25M.1A.SL.TZ1.9).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Every option containing II is wrong; D (all three) was the common belief.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: D assumes BF3 obeys the octet; B recognises boron has six electrons.

3_novel_application.short: Three look-alike AX3 formulas hide one electron-deficient centre.
3_novel_application.why: The formula type is the same but the central atom's group differs, and the group decides whether a lone pair is left.
3_novel_application.avoid: Judging by the formula pattern instead of the central atom.
3_novel_application.disguise: All three are AX3 halides, so they look identical in pattern.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Check the central atom's group: group 13 with three bonds gives 6 electrons; group 15 keeps a lone pair, giving 8.

4_command_terms.short: MCQ: judge each statement, then pick the combination.
4_command_terms.why: Roman-numeral items reward judging each molecule separately; one wrong call changes the letter.
4_command_terms.avoid: Choosing a letter after checking only one molecule.
4_command_terms.demands: Decide yes or no for each of I, II and III.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing for the letter.

5_time_efficiency.short: The central atom's group number settles it in seconds.
5_time_efficiency.why: Halogens with one bond always have octets, so only the central atom can fail.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Drawing every lone pair on nine halogen atoms.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No need for full Lewis formulas with every fluorine and chlorine lone pair.

6_data_booklet.short: No booklet table helps; use group numbers.
6_data_booklet.why: Valence electrons equal the group's last digit, which is the only data needed.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Searching the booklet for octet exceptions; none is listed.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Periodic table group: B has 3 valence electrons, N and P 5, F and Cl 7.
6_data_booklet.memorise: The octet rule and its exceptions (B and Be with fewer than eight) are NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: Strike every option that includes BF3.
7_elimination.why: Once BF3 fails, only one option leaves it out.
7_elimination.avoid: Second-guessing PCl3 as an expanded octet; it has only three bonds.

definitely_wrong.rule: Includes II: B in BF3 has only six electrons.
Includes II.
Includes II.

walkthrough.answer: B. In NF3 and PCl3 the central N or P has three bonds plus one lone pair (8 electrons). In BF3, boron has only three bonding pairs (6 electrons), so it is electron-deficient.

cards.title: Explain a shape: count domains and lone pairs on the central atom

walkthrough.question: Hydrogen cyanide, HCN, is a volatile liquid; H is bonded to C, and C is bonded to N. State the molecular geometry of HCN and explain it without using hybridization. [2]
walkthrough.key_idea: Two domains on C, no lone pairs: maximum separation gives linear.
walkthrough.question_type: VSEPR: state and explain molecular geometry
walkthrough.careful: Name the domains on the central atom, including zero lone pairs.
procedure: Draw the Lewis formula with all lone pairs.
Identify the central atom.
Count electron domains on it; a multiple bond counts once.
Count how many of those domains are lone pairs.
Name the electron domain geometry, then the molecular geometry.
Explain: domains repel and get as far apart as possible.
tricks: Always write 'X bonding domains and Y lone pairs on the central atom'.
A triple bond is one domain: HCN, CO2 and C2H2 are linear.
if_lost: Which atom sits in the middle of HCN?
How many atoms is carbon bonded to?
Does a triple bond count as one domain or three?
Does carbon have any electrons left as a lone pair?

1_context.short: Explaining a shape needs the domain count, not just the name.
1_context.why: 'Explain' carries a second mark only for the cause, so remembering 'linear' gets half the marks.
1_context.avoid: Saying the atoms want to be far apart; repulsion is between electron domains (05M.2.HL.TZ0.7).
1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.2.4: VSEPR predicts shapes from repulsion of electron domains around a central atom.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books give a shape table; exams want the reasoning: number of domains and lone pairs on the central atom.

2_markscheme_logic.short: M1 linear; M2 two domains on carbon, no lone pairs.
2_markscheme_logic.why: The markscheme accepts either two electron domains or two bonding pairs and no lone pairs; the repulsion wording is optional.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Stopping at 'linear, 180°'; the main loss was not explaining with domains (25M.2.HL.6215.1 examiner).
trigger_phrases: two electron domains around the central atom
two bonding pairs and no lone pairs
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: 'Linear' with no domain count earns M1 only; bent, trigonal planar or tetrahedral earn nothing.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Full credit adds the domain count on carbon; most candidates lost M2 here.

3_novel_application.short: A triple bond still counts as one domain.
3_novel_application.why: All the electrons of a multiple bond sit in one region between the same two atoms, so they act as one domain.
3_novel_application.avoid: Putting a lone pair on carbon, which leads to bent (25M.2.SL.TZ2.1).
3_novel_application.disguise: The triple bond tempts you to count extra domains and answer tetrahedral or trigonal.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Domains = atoms bonded to the centre + lone pairs on the centre; bond order never changes the count.

4_command_terms.short: State and explain: one mark name, one mark reason.
4_command_terms.why: State needs only the name; explain needs the cause in VSEPR terms.
4_command_terms.avoid: Mentioning sp hybridization: the question forbids it, so it earns nothing.
4_command_terms.demands: Name the geometry, then give its cause through the domains on carbon.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Per point: M1 geometry, M2 domains and lone pairs on the central atom.

5_time_efficiency.short: One sentence with the domain count gets the second mark.
5_time_efficiency.why: The markscheme needs the number of domains, not a long repulsion essay.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Writing about orbitals or bond strength.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip the bond angle discussion and any hybridization.

6_data_booklet.short: Nothing in the booklet helps; shapes are memorised.
6_data_booklet.why: Only valence electron counts are needed, and they come from group numbers.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking up bond lengths; they don't decide the shape.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Group numbers give valence electrons: H 1, C 4, N 5.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Domains to geometry (2 linear, 3 trigonal planar, 4 tetrahedral) is NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: Any bent or planar answer for HCN is out.
7_elimination.why: Carbon uses all four valence electrons in bonds, so no lone pair can bend it.
7_elimination.avoid: Counting the triple bond as three domains.

definitely_wrong.rule: Bent needs a lone pair on the centre; C has none.
The question bans it.
VSEPR is about repulsion between electron domains.

walkthrough.answer: Linear [1]. The central carbon has two electron domains (a single bond to H and a triple bond to N) and no lone pairs; they repel and sit as far apart as possible, at 180° [1].

1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.2.4 VSEPR: shapes from repulsion of electron domains around a central atom.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books give a shape table; markschemes give the second mark only for naming the domains and lone pairs on the central atom.

trigger_phrases: two electron domains around the central atom
two bonding pairs and no lone pairs

cards.title: Electron domain geometry vs molecular geometry

walkthrough.question: Sulfur dioxide, SO2, has sulfur as the central atom bonded to two oxygen atoms. Deduce (a) its electron domain geometry and (b) its molecular geometry. [2]
walkthrough.key_idea: Three domains on S, one a lone pair: trigonal planar domains, bent molecule.
walkthrough.question_type: VSEPR: electron domain vs molecular geometry
walkthrough.careful: Domain geometry includes lone pairs; molecular geometry does not.
procedure: Draw the Lewis formula; check lone pairs on the centre.
Count domains on the centre: bonded atoms plus lone pairs.
Domain count gives the electron domain geometry.
Ignore lone-pair positions; describe where the atoms sit.
Name that arrangement as the molecular geometry.
tricks: No lone pair on the centre? Both geometries have the same name.
Three domains with one lone pair is always bent.
if_lost: How many valence electrons does sulfur have?
After bonding to both O atoms, does S keep a lone pair?
Which geometry counts lone pairs, and which counts only atoms?

1_context.short: Two geometries asked: one with lone pairs, one without.
1_context.why: The syllabus separates the two terms, so each gets its own mark and must be named separately.
1_context.avoid: Guessing pairs like 'linear and bent' (25M.2.HL.6221.10 examiner).
1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.2.4: predict the electron domain geometry and the molecular geometry for up to four domains.
1_context.textbook_gap: Many books name only the molecular shape; exams ask for both in separate boxes.

2_markscheme_logic.short: One mark each: trigonal planar; bent, V-shaped or angular.
2_markscheme_logic.why: ECF from the candidate's own Lewis formula means a consistent wrong drawing can still score the geometries.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Missing the S lone pair in the Lewis formula, then answering linear (25M.2.HL.6221.10).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: ECF applies from the Lewis formula; guessed or contradictory pairs score nothing.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Full credit names the domain arrangement including the lone pair, then the shape of the atoms alone.

3_novel_application.short: Octet or expanded Lewis formula: still three domains.
3_novel_application.why: Both drawings give S two bonded atoms plus one lone pair, so the geometry doesn't change.
3_novel_application.avoid: Writing 'bent linear', which is not an accepted shape (09N.2.SL.TZ0.2).
3_novel_application.disguise: SO2 can be drawn with an expanded octet or with formal charges, so the drawings look different.
3_novel_application.heuristic: A double bond and a single bond are each one domain; only the lone-pair count matters.

4_command_terms.short: Deduce: reach both names from your own Lewis formula.
4_command_terms.why: Deduce asks for the conclusion only; no explanation mark is on offer here.
4_command_terms.avoid: Writing an explanation instead of the two names.
4_command_terms.demands: Give the electron domain geometry and the molecular geometry.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Per point: one mark per geometry, ECF from the Lewis formula.

5_time_efficiency.why: The domain count gives the first name; removing lone pairs gives the second.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Re-deriving the Lewis formula for each part.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No bond angle or explanation is needed unless asked.

6_data_booklet.short: Not in the booklet; group numbers only.
6_data_booklet.why: S in group 16 has six valence electrons: two double bonds use four, one lone pair remains.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Group 16: S has 6 valence electrons, the same as O.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Domain geometries and molecular shape names are NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.why: The molecular shape ignores the lone pair's position, so it can't match the domain geometry.

definitely_wrong.rule: S has a lone pair, so the names must differ.
Linear needs no lone pair on S.
Only three domains on S.

cards.title: Five and six domains: place the lone pairs

walkthrough.question:
Xenon tetrachloride is XeCl4. Which pair gives its electron domain geometry and its molecular geometry?
A. octahedral; tetrahedral
B. octahedral; square planar
C. tetrahedral; tetrahedral
D. tetrahedral; square planar
walkthrough.key_idea: Xe: four bonds plus two lone pairs = six domains; lone pairs opposite.
walkthrough.question_type: VSEPR: electron domain vs molecular geometry
walkthrough.careful: Xe has eight valence electrons; four remain as two lone pairs.
procedure: Count valence electrons on the central atom.
Subtract one per single bond to a halogen.
Halve the remainder to get lone pairs.
Bonds plus lone pairs give the electron domain geometry.
Place lone pairs: opposite in octahedral, equatorial in trigonal bipyramidal.
Name the shape from atom positions only.
tricks: Six domains with two lone pairs: always square planar (XeF4, ICl4−).
Five domains: lone pairs go equatorial, so SF4 is seesaw and XeF2 linear.
if_lost: How many valence electrons does xenon have?
How many of them are used in four Xe–Cl bonds?
How many lone pairs remain, so how many domains in total?

1_context.short: HL expanded octet: up to six domains on the centre.
1_context.why: Period 5 xenon can hold more than eight electrons, so all its electrons count as domains.
1_context.avoid: Counting four bonds as four domains: XeF4 was often given as tetrahedral (06M.2.HL.TZ0.7).
1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.2.13: expanded octets; deduce electron domain and molecular geometry for five and six domains.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books list SF6, PCl5 and XeF4; exams pick unlisted analogues such as XeCl4 or ICl4− (07N.1.HL.TZ0.12).

2_markscheme_logic.short: B: octahedral domains, square planar molecule.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Two lone pairs repel most when far apart, so they take opposite positions and leave the four Cl in one plane.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Mixing up domain and molecular geometry, which is worse with six pairs (25M.1A.HL.6213.9 examiner).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Any option with tetrahedral domains counts only bonds and ignores two lone pairs.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: A gets the domains right but names the molecule by bond count; B removes the lone pairs from the octahedron.

3_novel_application.short: A noble gas as the centre is treated like any atom.
3_novel_application.why: Valence electrons minus bonding electrons, halved, gives lone pairs for any centre, noble gas or not.
3_novel_application.avoid: Deciding Xe can't bond, so guessing.
3_novel_application.disguise: A noble gas centre looks as if it can't bond at all.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Lone pairs = (valence electrons − bonds) ÷ 2; for ions adjust by the charge first.

4_command_terms.short: MCQ: two names per option; both must be right.
4_command_terms.why: Each option pairs two geometries, so check each half separately.
4_command_terms.demands: Choose the correct domain geometry and molecular geometry pair.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Electron count gives six domains; geometry follows.
5_time_efficiency.why: One subtraction and one halving settle both columns.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Drawing all twelve Cl lone pairs.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No 3D sketch is needed in an MCQ.

6_data_booklet.short: Not in the booklet; group numbers only.
6_data_booklet.why: Xe is in group 18 (8 valence electrons) and Cl needs one bond.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking for shape data in the booklet.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Group 18 Xe: 8 valence electrons; group 17 Cl: one bond each.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Five- and six-domain shapes (trigonal bipyramidal, seesaw, T-shaped, square pyramidal, square planar) are NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: Tetrahedral domains are impossible with six electron pairs.
7_elimination.why: Four bonds plus two lone pairs is six domains, so the domain geometry must be octahedral.
7_elimination.avoid: Picking D because square planar sounds right.

definitely_wrong.rule: Four bonds plus two lone pairs can't be tetrahedral domains.
Square planar never comes from four domains.
Tetrahedral is not a shape that comes from six domains.

walkthrough.answer: B. Xe has 8 valence electrons; 4 form bonds to Cl and 4 remain as 2 lone pairs. Six domains give an octahedral arrangement; the lone pairs sit opposite each other, leaving the four Cl atoms in a square plane.

cards.title: Rank bond angles: domains first, lone pairs second

walkthrough.question:
Put C2H4, CH4, NH3 and H2O in order of decreasing bond angle (largest first).
A. NH3, H2O, C2H4, CH4
B. H2O, C2H4, CH4, NH3
C. C2H4, CH4, NH3, H2O
D. CH4, NH3, H2O, C2H4
walkthrough.key_idea: Fewer domains give wider angles; each lone pair closes the angle further.
walkthrough.question_type: VSEPR: rank or predict bond angles
walkthrough.careful: Ethene's carbon has three domains: 120°, not 109.5°.
procedure: Find the number of domains on each central atom.
Assign the base angle: 2 → 180°, 3 → 120°, 4 → 109.5°.
Count lone pairs on each central atom.
Take about 2.5° off per lone pair at four domains.
Rank the values in the order asked.
tricks: Four-domain series: 109.5°, 107°, 104.5° for 0, 1, 2 lone pairs.
Any carbon in C=C or C=O (about 120°) beats every four-domain centre.
if_lost: How many domains surround each carbon in ethene?
Which molecules have lone pairs on the central atom?
Does a lone pair widen or narrow the bond angle?

1_context.short: Guidance says lone pairs and multiple bonds change bond angles.

2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Starting with CH4 as if 109.5° were the largest possible angle.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: An order that puts NH3 or H2O above CH4 ignores lone-pair repulsion.

cards.title: Explain molecular polarity: polar bonds plus non-cancelling geometry

walkthrough.question: Sulfur dioxide, SO2, is a bent molecule with sulfur at the centre. Explain why SO2 is polar. [2]
walkthrough.key_idea: Polar S–O bonds at an angle: dipoles don't cancel, so net dipole.
walkthrough.question_type: Molecular polarity: explain polar or non-polar
walkthrough.careful: Say the bond dipoles don't cancel because of the bent shape.
procedure: Compare the electronegativities of the bonded atoms.
Any difference: the bond is polar; mark δ+ and δ−.
Deduce the molecular geometry by VSEPR.
Decide whether the bond dipoles cancel by symmetry.
No cancellation: net dipole, molecule polar.
tricks: Two sentences, two marks: 'bonds polar', then 'dipoles don't cancel because…'.
Identical terminal atoms with no lone pair on the centre: non-polar (CO2, CH4, BF3).
if_lost: Which is more electronegative, S or O?
What is the shape of SO2?
When two bond dipoles point at an angle, do they cancel?

1_context.short: Polarity needs both bond polarity and molecular geometry.
1_context.why: The syllabus statement joins two ideas, and the markscheme gives one mark to each.
1_context.avoid: Explaining polarity only by the lone pair on S (25M.2.SL.TZ3.7).
1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.2.6: molecular polarity depends on both bond polarity and molecular geometry.

2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Putting δ− on S, or saying the EN difference is too small (25M.2.HL.6221.10 examiner).
trigger_phrases: bond dipoles do not cancel / net dipole
bonds at an angle less than 180°
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Linking the dipole to the S lone pair alone gets no M2; δ− on S is wrong.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Most scored one or zero; full credit needs the geometry reason for non-cancellation.

3_novel_application.short: SO2 looks like CO2, but the lone pair bends it.
3_novel_application.why: In CO2 the two dipoles are at 180° and cancel; in bent SO2 they add to a net dipole.
3_novel_application.avoid: Calling SO2 non-polar by analogy with CO2.
3_novel_application.disguise: The formula SO2 looks like CO2, which is non-polar.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Check both: polar bonds AND an asymmetric shape. Both are needed for a polar molecule.

4_command_terms.short: Explain: give the cause, in two linked statements.
4_command_terms.why: Each statement is a separate marking point, so a single word ('bent') isn't an explanation.
4_command_terms.avoid: Writing only 'SO2 is bent, so polar'.
4_command_terms.demands: Why the bonds are polar and why their dipoles don't cancel.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Per point: M1 bond polarity, M2 non-cancellation from the shape.

5_time_efficiency.short: Two sentences and a δ-labelled sketch are enough.
5_time_efficiency.why: Both marks need ideas, not length.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip electronegativity numbers; saying O is more electronegative is enough.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 9: compare the electronegativities of S and O.
6_data_booklet.why: The more electronegative atom takes δ−, so the booklet decides where the charges go.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Assuming the central atom is δ−.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Section 9 lists electronegativity for each element; read S and O.
6_data_booklet.memorise: The rule that symmetric shapes cancel bond dipoles is NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: Rule out δ− on S and 'difference too small'.
7_elimination.why: O is more electronegative than S, and any difference makes the bond polar.
7_elimination.avoid: Thinking polar bonds need a large difference.

definitely_wrong.target: S given as the δ− atom
definitely_wrong.rule: O is more electronegative than S.
Any S–O difference makes the bonds polar.

definitely_wrong.target: Lone pair alone as the reason
definitely_wrong.rule: Must say bond dipoles don't cancel.

walkthrough.answer: M1: the S–O bonds are polar because O is more electronegative than S. M2: the molecule is bent (angle less than 180°), so the bond dipoles don't cancel and there is a net dipole; S is δ+ and both O atoms are δ−.

1_context.textbook_gap: Books show dipole arrows cancelling; exams want two separate statements: the bonds are polar, then the shape stops them cancelling.

trigger_phrases: bond dipoles do not cancel / net dipole
δ+ on S and δ− on O
trap_boundaries: The lone pair alone as the cause gets no credit (25M.2.HL.6221.10 examiner).
δ− on S is wrong (25M.2.HL.6221.10 examiner).
ECF applies from the stated molecular geometry (25M.2.HL.6221.10).
For non-polar molecules, say the bond dipoles cancel (04M.2.SL.TZ0.3).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: One mark for bond polarity is common; the second needs the geometry argument that the dipoles add up.

disguises: Formula pairs like SO2 vs CO2, or H2S vs CO2 (04M.2.SL.TZ0.3).
CH4, C6H6 and CO2 distractors with polar bonds but symmetric shapes (25M.1A.HL.6213.7).

3_novel_application.heuristic: Polar = polar bonds AND an asymmetric shape. Isotopes change mass, not electron distribution.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Two marks, one per point: bond polarity, then geometry and net dipole.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip numbers; state which atom is more electronegative.

rules: Symmetric shape with identical terminal atoms (CO2, CH4, BF3, C6H6): non-polar.
Swapping isotopes never changes a dipole moment.
Saying the S–O difference is too small for polarity is wrong.

cards.title: Compare boiling points: find the intermolecular force one has and the other lacks

walkthrough.question:
Ammonia, NH3, boils at a much higher temperature than phosphine, PH3. Which attraction explains this?
A. Covalent bonds
B. Dipole–dipole forces
C. London (dispersion) forces
D. Hydrogen bonds
walkthrough.key_idea: H on N can hydrogen bond; H on P cannot.
walkthrough.careful: Boiling never breaks covalent bonds; compare forces between molecules.
procedure: List IMFs for each substance: London forces always present.
Add dipole–dipole if the molecule is polar.
Add hydrogen bonding if H is bonded to N, O or F.
Find the force one substance has and the other lacks.
Name it and say it is stronger.
tricks: Lighter molecule boils much higher? Look for H on N, O or F.
At similar mass: London < dipole–dipole < hydrogen bonding.
if_lost: Which of the two molecules is heavier?
If the heavier one boils lower, what extra force must the other have?
Which atoms must H be bonded to for hydrogen bonding?

1_context.short: IMF ranking at comparable mass; here size and H-bonding compete.
1_context.why: PH3 is heavier, so it has stronger London forces, but hydrogen bonding in NH3 outweighs that.
1_context.avoid: Weighing PH3's larger London forces as dominant; at SL this question split candidates evenly (25M.1A.SL.TZ1.4).
1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.2.9: at comparable molar mass, London < dipole–dipole < hydrogen bonding.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books rank forces at equal mass; exams pair a lighter H-bonded molecule with a heavier one.

2_markscheme_logic.short: D: hydrogen bonds between NH3 molecules.
2_markscheme_logic.why: N is very electronegative and has a lone pair, so N–H···N attractions form between molecules; P is too weakly electronegative.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Choosing A: covalent bonds stay intact on boiling (05M.1.SL.TZ0.11).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Covalent bonds are inside molecules and are not broken on boiling.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: C is tempting because PH3 is larger; D names the force NH3 has and PH3 lacks.

3_novel_application.short: Heavier compound boils lower: size isn't the deciding factor.
3_novel_application.why: Hydrogen bonding is much stronger than the extra London forces from one bigger atom.
3_novel_application.avoid: Applying 'bigger means higher boiling point' without checking for H-bonding.
3_novel_application.disguise: Same group, similar formula, and the heavier one boils lower.
3_novel_application.heuristic: When the lighter one boils higher, look for H on N, O or F.

4_command_terms.short: MCQ: pick the force that causes the difference.
4_command_terms.why: The question asks what makes NH3 higher, so the answer must be something NH3 has extra.
4_command_terms.avoid: Choosing a force both molecules share.
4_command_terms.demands: Identify the attraction responsible for the higher boiling point.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Check H on N, O, F first.
5_time_efficiency.why: That one check settles most boiling point MCQs.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip estimating molar masses.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 9: N is far more electronegative than H; P isn't.
6_data_booklet.why: Hydrogen bonding needs H attached to a very electronegative atom.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Assuming any H-containing molecule hydrogen bonds.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Section 9 electronegativities: compare N, P and H.
6_data_booklet.memorise: That only N, O and F give hydrogen bonds is NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: Covalent bonds and London forces can't explain NH3's higher value.
7_elimination.why: Boiling leaves covalent bonds intact, and London forces favour the bigger PH3.
7_elimination.avoid: Picking dipole–dipole as a safe middle answer.

definitely_wrong.rule: Boiling separates molecules; covalent bonds stay intact.
London forces favour the larger PH3, so they can't explain NH3 boiling higher.
Not the specific strong attraction NH3 has and PH3 lacks.

walkthrough.answer: D. In NH3, H is bonded to the highly electronegative N, which has a lone pair, so hydrogen bonds form between molecules. P is not electronegative enough, so PH3 has only weaker London (and weak dipole–dipole) forces despite its larger mass.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.2.8 deduce IMF types from structure; S2.2.9 at comparable mass, London < dipole–dipole < hydrogen bonding; explain volatility and solubility.

trigger_phrases: N2 only London; HCN dipole–dipole (and London)
dipole–dipole forces stronger than London forces
stronger intermolecular forces in the polar compound

2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial credit names the forces; full credit also says which is stronger and links it to the boiling point.

disguises: Heavier molecule boils lower (PH3 vs NH3).
Isomers: ethanol vs methoxymethane (11M.2.HL.TZ2.4).
Solubility in water through H-bonds, e.g. ethanal or propanone (03N.2.HL.TZ0.7, 19M.2.SL.TZ2.1).
3_novel_application.heuristic: List forces for both, find the difference, name it and say it is stronger.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Per point: the forces in each substance, then their relative strength.

rules: Covalent bonds are never broken when a molecular substance boils.
Hydrogen bonds are weaker than covalent bonds (05N.1.SL.TZ0.9).
Hydrogens bonded to carbon never form hydrogen bonds.

cards.title: Hydrogen bond: H on N/O/F attracted to another molecule's N/O/F

walkthrough.question: Chains of nylon 6,6 contain N–H groups and C=O groups in their amide links. Hydrogen bonding between neighbouring chains makes the polymer strong. Outline how a hydrogen bond forms. [2]
walkthrough.key_idea: δ+ H on N/O/F attracts an N/O/F atom on another molecule.
walkthrough.careful: The hydrogen bond is between molecules, not within one chain.
procedure: Find H covalently bonded to N, O or F.
State that this H is δ+ because its partner is electronegative.
Find an N, O or F with a lone pair on a neighbour.
State that the δ+ H is attracted to that atom.
On a diagram: dotted line from H to that atom.
tricks: Two marks, two halves: the H and its partner, then the neighbour's atom.
Annotating nylon: N–H of one chain to the O of C=O on the other.
if_lost: Which hydrogens in nylon are bonded to an electronegative atom?

Which atom on the other chain could attract it?

I. Graphite
II. Diamond
III. Graphene
A. I and II only
B. I and III only
C. II and III only
D. I, II and III
walkthrough.key_idea: Conduction needs delocalized electrons: three-bonded carbons have one, diamond none.
walkthrough.careful: In diamond every valence electron is fixed in four bonds.
procedure: Recall each structure: bonds per atom.
Four bonds per C or Si: all electrons localized.
Three bonds per C: one electron per atom delocalized.
Mobile electrons conduct; localized electrons don't.
For melting point: strong covalent bonds broken, so very high.
tricks: Three-bonded carbon (graphite, graphene) conducts; four-bonded (diamond) does not.

if_lost: How many carbons is each carbon bonded to in diamond?
And in graphite and graphene?

1_context.why: The guidance links each property to bonding pattern, so conductivity follows from how many bonds each carbon forms.
1_context.avoid: Treating 'carbon network' as one property set for all allotropes.
1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.2.7: structures and properties of Si, SiO2, diamond, graphite, fullerenes and graphene.

2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Not separating localized electrons in diamond from delocalized ones in graphite (02M.2.HL.TZ0.8).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Any option including diamond is wrong.

cards.title: Resonance: one bond length for equivalent bonds, from the booklet

walkthrough.question: Sulfur trioxide, SO3, has several possible Lewis structures. Using data booklet bond lengths (section 11 in the 2025 booklet; the paper cites the old section 10), predict the length of each sulfur–oxygen bond in pm. [1]
walkthrough.key_idea: Delocalization makes all S–O bonds equal and shorter than a single bond.
walkthrough.question_type: Resonance: predict bond length or order
walkthrough.careful: Give one value for all the bonds, never two.
procedure: Draw the possible resonance structures.
Note that equivalent bonds differ between the structures.
Delocalization makes all equivalent bonds identical.
Look up single and double bond lengths in section 11.
Predict one value: shorter than single, near or between.
tricks: Resonance means one length for all equivalent bonds.
Average bond order sets the position: nitrate 4/3, benzene 1.5.
if_lost: Are the three S–O bonds in SO3 different or identical?
Which section 11 values could bracket the answer?
Should your answer be one number or several?

1_context.short: Resonance turns into a measurable result: equal bond lengths.
1_context.why: Delocalized electrons spread over all equivalent bonds, so none is a pure single or double bond.
1_context.avoid: Quoting two booklet values (24M.2.SL.TZ2.2: 121 and 148 pm scored nothing).

1_context.textbook_gap: Books draw resonance arrows; exams want a number from booklet data.

2_markscheme_logic.short: One value, less than 161 pm, accepted range 121–161 pm.
2_markscheme_logic.why: The real value is 142 pm; any single value shorter than the S–O single bond shows you understand delocalization.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Giving two lengths: the mark is withheld (24N.2.HL.TZ0.4).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Two bond length values get no mark; no ECF from your Lewis structures.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Full credit is one value below the single-bond length; listing single and double values scores zero.

3_novel_application.short: Octet and expanded-octet drawings both suggest unequal bonds.
3_novel_application.why: Whatever structure you draw, the real molecule has three identical delocalized S–O bonds.
3_novel_application.avoid: Adding bond lengths together, as some did for ozone (24M.2.HL.TZ2.2).
3_novel_application.disguise: SO3 can be drawn with or without an expanded octet, and the bonds look different.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Equivalent atoms bonded to one centre in resonance mean identical bonds.

4_command_terms.short: Predict: one expected value, no working needed.
4_command_terms.why: Predict asks for a result, so the number alone earns the mark.
4_command_terms.avoid: Explaining delocalization instead of giving the value.
4_command_terms.demands: An expected S–O length in pm.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing; one value only.

5_time_efficiency.short: Two booklet lookups and one number.
5_time_efficiency.why: The accepted range is wide, so no bond order calculation is needed.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 11: S–O 161 pm single, O=S 143 pm double.

6_data_booklet.avoid: Using the old 'section 10' reference in the 2025 booklet.
6_data_booklet.memorise: That resonance gives equal, intermediate bond lengths is NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: Two values, or any value above 161 pm, is wrong.
7_elimination.why: Delocalization adds bond order, so bonds must be shorter than single and all the same.
7_elimination.avoid: Giving the single-bond value as a safe answer.

definitely_wrong.rule: Resonance makes all three bonds identical.
Delocalized bonds are shorter than the single bond.
A length is per bond, never added (24M.2.HL.TZ2.2).

walkthrough.answer: All three S–O bonds have the same length, less than the S–O single bond (161 pm), e.g. about 145 pm. The markscheme accepts any single value above 121 pm and below 161 pm (actual 142 pm). Giving two values scores zero.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.2.11 resonance and delocalization; S2.2.2 more shared pairs give shorter, stronger bonds.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books draw resonance; exams make you turn it into one bond length from booklet data.

Old papers cite section 10; the 2025 booklet uses section 11.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No need to compute bond order.

rules: Resonance never gives different lengths for equivalent bonds.
An answer longer than the single bond is wrong.
Between the same two atoms, shorter bonds are stronger.

Bond length prediction mean 0.33/1; quite difficult.

Some added single bond lengths for ozone.

cards.title: Benzene: pick evidence that contradicts Kekulé

walkthrough.question:
Kekulé proposed that benzene has alternating C–C single and C=C double bonds. Which observation disproves this structure?
A. The formula of benzene is C6H6.
B. Benzene is unsaturated.
C. All carbon–carbon bonds in benzene have the same length.
D. Benzene can be hydrogenated.
walkthrough.key_idea: Kekulé predicts two bond lengths; one observed C–C length disproves it.
walkthrough.careful: The evidence must contradict Kekulé, not just fit benzene.
procedure: Write down what the Kekulé structure predicts.
For each statement, ask: does Kekulé predict it too?
Keep only evidence Kekulé can't explain.
Physical: one C–C length; hydrogenation less exothermic than expected.
Chemical: substitution favoured over addition.
tricks: A fact also true of cyclohexatriene can't disprove Kekulé.
Benzene's bond length lies between C–C 154 and C=C 134 pm.
if_lost: What bond lengths would alternating single and double bonds give?
Which statements would also be true of Kekulé's structure?
Which observation conflicts with two kinds of bond?

1_context.short: HL: discuss benzene's structure from physical and chemical evidence.
1_context.why: Evidence only counts against Kekulé if his structure can't explain it.
1_context.avoid: Picking any true fact about benzene.
1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.2.12: benzene, C6H6, has resonance; discuss its structure from physical and chemical evidence.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books list the evidence; exams ask which single fact actually contradicts Kekulé.

2_markscheme_logic.short: C: equal C–C lengths contradict alternating bonds.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Alternating bonds would give two lengths; one length shows the π electrons are delocalized round the ring.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Writing 'all bonds same length' without saying C–C (19M.2.HL.TZ1.2).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Unsaturation and hydrogenation fit Kekulé too, so they don't disprove it.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: B and D describe unsaturation that Kekulé predicts; C is the one fact he can't explain.

3_novel_application.short: All four statements are true; only one contradicts.
3_novel_application.why: The test is not 'is it true' but 'would Kekulé's molecule do this too'.
3_novel_application.avoid: Treating 'unsaturated' as evidence against double bonds.
3_novel_application.disguise: Every option is a correct fact about benzene.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask 'would cyclohexatriene also do this?' If yes, it isn't disproof.

4_command_terms.short: MCQ: choose the observation that disproves the model.
4_command_terms.why: Disproving needs a contradiction, not agreement.
4_command_terms.avoid: Choosing a fact that merely describes benzene.
4_command_terms.demands: Identify evidence incompatible with the Kekulé structure.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Strike every fact that Kekulé also explains.
5_time_efficiency.why: Three options fit Kekulé, so they go immediately.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip enthalpy calculations; not needed here.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 11: Kekulé predicts both 154 and 134 pm.
6_data_booklet.why: The booklet's single and double C–C lengths show what two bond types would look like.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Expecting benzene's own value in the booklet.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Benzene's actual C–C length (about 140 pm) is NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: Formula, unsaturation and hydrogenation all fit Kekulé.
7_elimination.why: Cyclohexatriene would have the same formula, C=C bonds and addition reactions.
7_elimination.avoid: Choosing D because hydrogenation 'involves double bonds'.

definitely_wrong.rule: The Kekulé structure is also C6H6.
Kekulé has C=C bonds, so it is unsaturated too.
Kekulé's C=C bonds could also be hydrogenated.

walkthrough.answer: C. Kekulé's structure would have two C–C bond lengths (single and double); all the C–C bonds in benzene are the same length, which shows delocalized π electrons. A, B and D would also be true of Kekulé's structure.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.2.12 benzene's resonance; discuss its structure from physical and chemical evidence.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books list the evidence; exams ask which fact contradicts the Kekulé model, and want precise wording.

trigger_phrases: all C–C bonds the same length
bond length between single and double
trap_boundaries: Specify C–C bonds, not 'all bonds in benzene' (19M.2.HL.TZ1.2).
Facts that Kekulé also predicts don't count as disproof (25M.1A.HL.6207.13).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Full credit names an observation Kekulé can't explain, worded precisely.

disguises: Options that are true facts which Kekulé also satisfies.
Bond length data read from section 11.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Would cyclohexatriene do this too? If so, it isn't disproof.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark per valid, precisely worded piece of evidence.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No enthalpy arithmetic for an MCQ.

6_data_booklet.hack: C–C 154 and C=C 134 pm: Kekulé predicts both; a single intermediate value disproves him. Benzene's own value is NOT in the booklet.

rules: Formula, unsaturation and addition reactions can't disprove Kekulé.
Evidence must contradict, not just describe.

evidence.note: Evidence against Kekulé: all C–C bonds equal length; answer C.
Lost marks for 'all bonds same length' rather than 'all C–C bonds'.

cards.title: Formal charge: bookkeeping per atom, then prefer closest to zero

walkthrough.question:
The Lewis formula of the nitrate ion, NO3−, is shown with N bonded to three O atoms: one by a double bond and two by single bonds. N has no lone pairs. What is the formal charge on nitrogen?
A. −3
B. −1
C. +1
D. +3
walkthrough.key_idea: Formal charge = valence − non-bonding electrons − half the bonding electrons.
walkthrough.question_type: Formal charge: calculate and choose Lewis formula
walkthrough.careful: Count lone-pair electrons in full but only half the bonding ones.
procedure: Note the atom's valence electrons (group number).
Count its non-bonding electrons (two per lone pair).
Count its bonding electrons, then halve.
Formal charge = valence − non-bonding − half bonding.
Check the formal charges add up to the species' charge.
Preferred Lewis formula: formal charges closest to zero.
tricks: Shortcut: formal charge = valence − (lone-pair electrons + number of bonds).
N with four bonds and no lone pair is always +1 (NH4+, nitrate).
if_lost: How many valence electrons does nitrogen have?
Does nitrogen have any lone pairs in this structure?
How many bonds does N form, counting a double bond as two?

1_context.short: HL formal charge: one atom at a time from the drawn structure.
1_context.why: Formal charge compares an atom's electrons in the structure with the free atom, so it is calculated per atom.
1_context.avoid: Spreading the ion's −1 charge over the atoms; about 55% got this right (25M.1A.HL.6219.9).
1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.2.14: calculate formal charges and use them to pick the preferred Lewis formula.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books teach the formula; exams combine it with resonance and choosing the preferred structure.

2_markscheme_logic.why: N has 5 valence electrons, no lone pairs and 8 bonding electrons (4 bonds): 5 − 0 − 8/2 = +1.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Confusing formal charge with the ion's charge or with oxidation state.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: −1 is the whole ion's charge; +5 would be the oxidation state.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: B gives the ion's overall charge to N; C does the electron bookkeeping.

3_novel_application.short: Resonance doesn't change N's formal charge.
3_novel_application.why: In every resonance form N has four bonds and no lone pair, so it is always +1.
3_novel_application.avoid: Formal charge errors when resonance structures are drawn (24M.2.HL.TZ2.2).
3_novel_application.disguise: The ion's charge and the resonance tempt you to share the charge evenly.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Calculate each atom separately, then check that the total equals the ion's charge.

4_command_terms.why: Only nitrogen's value is asked; the others are only for checking.
4_command_terms.avoid: Calculating all four atoms before answering.
4_command_terms.demands: Find the formal charge on N.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Valence minus lone electrons minus bonds.
5_time_efficiency.why: Counting bonds is the same as halving the bonding electrons and is faster.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Drawing every O lone pair again.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Ignore the other resonance forms.

6_data_booklet.short: Not in the booklet; group numbers only.
6_data_booklet.why: Only valence electron counts are needed: N 5, O 6.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking for a formal charge formula in the booklet.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Group number gives valence electrons: N 5, O 6.
6_data_booklet.memorise: The formal charge formula is NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: N has no lone pairs, so its formal charge can't be negative.
7_elimination.why: A negative formal charge needs more non-bonding electrons than the atom has; N here has none.

definitely_wrong.rule: −3 needs extra lone-pair electrons; N has none here.
That is the ion's overall charge, not N's formal charge.
Four bonds and no lone pair can only give +1 for N.

walkthrough.answer: C. N: 5 valence electrons, 0 non-bonding, 8 bonding electrons (four bonds), so 5 − 0 − 4 = +1. Check: the two single-bonded O are −1 each and the double-bonded O is 0, total −1, which equals the ion's charge.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.2.14 formal charge chooses the preferred Lewis formula among alternatives.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books teach the formula; exams mix it with expanded octets and resonance (24N.2.HL.TZ0.4, 25N.2.HL.6221.2).

trigger_phrases: formal charges zero / closest to zero, hence preferred
trap_boundaries: State the formal charges in each Lewis formula before choosing (25N.2.HL.6221.2).
Lewis formulas drawn with formal charges are accepted (25M.2.HL.6221.10).
Errors were common when resonance structures were drawn (24M.2.HL.TZ2.2).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial: naming the preferred formula. Full: formal charges for both formulas plus 'closest to zero'.

disguises: Octet vs expanded-octet structures for SO3, phosphates or ClO4−.
Atom-order alternatives such as NNO vs NON in N2O (25M.1A.HL.6207.10).
3_novel_application.heuristic: Calculate each atom, check the sum equals the charge, then prefer charges closest to zero.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark per correct set of formal charges; one mark for the choice with its reason.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Only calculate the atoms that differ between the structures.

6_data_booklet.hack: The formal charge formula is NOT in the booklet; only group numbers are needed.

rules: Formal charges must add up to the species' charge.
An atom with no lone pairs can't have a negative formal charge unless it is in group 13 or 14 (B with four bonds is −1).
Formal charge is not the oxidation state.

evidence.note: Formal charge of N in nitrate: +1; answer C.
Almost 55% identified the formal charge.
More stable Lewis structure decided by lowest formal charge.

cards.title: Count sigma and pi bonds: one σ per bond, extras are π

walkthrough.question:
But-2-enenitrile has the structure CH3–CH=CH–C≡N. How many π and σ bonds does one molecule contain?
A. 5 π, 2 σ
B. 5 π, 7 σ
C. 3 π, 4 σ
D. 3 π, 9 σ
walkthrough.key_idea: Every bond has one σ; a double adds one π, triple two.
walkthrough.question_type: Sigma and pi bonds: count in a molecule
walkthrough.careful: Count every C–H bond as sigma; they are easy to miss.
procedure: Draw the full structural formula with every H.
Count every atom-to-atom connection: each is one σ.
Add one π for each double bond.
Add two π for each triple bond.
Report the σ and π totals.
tricks: Non-ring molecule: σ = number of atoms − 1. Fails for rings: add one per ring.
Nitrile C≡N always gives 1 σ + 2 π.
if_lost: How many hydrogens are there, and which carbons hold them?
How many double and triple bonds does the molecule have?
Is a double bond one σ plus one π, or two π?

1_context.short: HL σ/π: head-on vs sideways overlap; counts from structure.
1_context.why: Every bond starts with one head-on σ overlap; extra pairs in multiple bonds come from sideways p overlap, which is π.
1_context.avoid: Thinking C=O is only a π bond (03M.1.HL.TZ0.14).
1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.2.15: σ bonds from head-on overlap; π bonds from sideways p-orbital overlap; deduce them in molecules.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books show orbital pictures; exams want fast, careful counts in an unfamiliar molecule.

2_markscheme_logic.why: σ: 5 C–H, 2 C–C, plus one σ in C=C and one in C≡N = 9. π: 1 + 2 = 3.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Counting each multiple bond's σ as a π.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Options with 5 π count every bond in the multiple bonds as π.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: A and B count all five bonds in C=C and C≡N as π; D splits them into σ and π correctly.

3_novel_application.short: The condensed formula hides the H atoms and triple bond.
3_novel_application.why: Writing the full structure shows the five hidden C–H σ bonds.
3_novel_application.disguise: A condensed name and formula instead of a drawn structure.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Expand to the full structure; C≡N always gives 1 σ + 2 π.

4_command_terms.short: MCQ with two columns: check the π column first.
4_command_terms.why: π is quick to count and already rules out two options.
4_command_terms.avoid: Mixing up the column order (π listed first here).
4_command_terms.demands: Total π and σ bonds in one molecule.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Atoms minus one gives σ; multiple bonds give π.
5_time_efficiency.why: In a molecule without rings every connection is one σ, and there are one fewer than the atoms.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No hybridization labels needed.

6_data_booklet.short: Nothing in the booklet needed; valences fix the structure.
6_data_booklet.why: C makes 4 bonds, N 3 and H 1, which confirms where the multiple bonds are.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Hunting the booklet for σ/π data.
6_data_booklet.pattern: No table needed; valences C 4, N 3, H 1 fix the structure.
6_data_booklet.memorise: What σ and π make up each multiple bond is NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: Ten atoms need nine σ bonds: only D fits.
7_elimination.why: A molecule with no rings has one fewer σ bond than atoms.

definitely_wrong.rule: 2 σ is far too few to join ten atoms.
4 σ ignores the five C–H bonds.
5 π needs more multiple bonds than one C=C and one C≡N.

walkthrough.answer: D. σ: 3 C–H on CH3, 1 C–H on each CH (2), 2 C–C single bonds, 1 σ in C=C and 1 σ in C≡N = 9. π: 1 from C=C and 2 from C≡N = 3.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.2.15 σ and π bonds: deduce their presence in organic and inorganic species.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books show orbital overlap diagrams; exams ask for totals in unfamiliar molecules and for the σ/π of a single atom.

trigger_phrases: sigma bonds: 2 AND pi bonds: 2 (HCN carbon)
each multiple bond contains one σ
trap_boundaries: HCN: σ and π counts are one combined mark (25M.2.HL.6215.1).
Some treat C=O as only a π bond (03M.1.HL.TZ0.14).
Read whether the count is for the molecule or one atom (03M.1.HL.TZ0.14).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Full credit separates every multiple bond into one σ plus the rest as π.

Count around one atom vs the whole molecule.

(NC)2CC(CN)2: 9 σ, 9 π; answer C.

cards.title: Hybridization of every atom, including terminal O in resonance

walkthrough.question:
In the carbonate ion, CO3^2−, what are the hybridizations of the carbon atom and of the oxygen atoms?
A. C sp2; O sp3
B. C sp2; O sp2
C. C sp3; O sp2
D. C sp3; O sp
walkthrough.key_idea: Count domains per atom; delocalized π makes every carbonate O sp2.
walkthrough.careful: Count the lone pairs on terminal O; don't default to sp3.
procedure: Draw the Lewis formula with all lone pairs.
For each atom asked, count domains: bonded atoms plus lone pairs.
2 domains sp; 3 domains sp2; 4 domains sp3.
An atom in a delocalized π system keeps a p orbital: sp2.
tricks: An atom with one double bond (C, N or O) is sp2.
Resonance: atoms sharing the delocalized π are sp2 in every form.
if_lost: How many domains does carbon have in carbonate?
In the C=O form, how many lone pairs does that oxygen carry?
Can an atom without a spare p orbital join a delocalized π system?

2_markscheme_logic.short: B: carbon sp2 and oxygen sp2.
2_markscheme_logic.why: The double-bonded O has two lone pairs plus one bonded atom, three domains. Delocalization needs a p orbital on every O, so all three are sp2.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Picking sp3 for O like in water; most candidates did, under a third were right (25M.1A.HL.6219.10).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: O as sp3 (option A) was the majority wrong answer.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: A treats each O like the O in water; B sees O's three domains and its part in the delocalized π.

3_novel_application.short: Terminal O in a resonance ion looks like water's oxygen.
3_novel_application.why: A single-bonded O− in one resonance form seems to have four domains, but delocalization needs an unhybridized p orbital.
3_novel_application.avoid: Ignoring lone pairs and calling O sp (25M.1A.HL.6213.10 examiner).
3_novel_application.disguise: A terminal atom in an ion with resonance.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Use the double-bonded form; three domains means sp2, and resonance keeps it sp2.

7_elimination.short: Planar carbonate rules out sp3 carbon at once.
7_elimination.why: Carbon has three domains and no lone pair, so it is trigonal planar and sp2.
7_elimination.avoid: Thinking the 2− charge adds domains to carbon.

definitely_wrong.rule: Carbon with three domains can't be sp3.
Carbon sp3 is impossible; O with lone pairs can't have only two domains.
An sp3 O has no spare p orbital for the delocalized π.

walkthrough.answer: B. Carbon has three domains (three O atoms, no lone pair), so sp2. The double-bonded O has two lone pairs and one bonded atom (three domains), so sp2; because the π bond is delocalized over all three O atoms, every O is sp2.
